# Common Practice

Common Practice is live at <https://withcommonpractice.com>, with its API at
<https://api.withcommonpractice.com>. The repository, packages, Workers, bindings,
Doppler project and active artwork now use the new name. Old website links redirect
with their path and query; the old API stays available for existing clients.
See the [cutover checklist](docs/exec-plans/common-practice-cutover-checklist.md)
for completed work, retained historical identifiers and the remaining external items.

A small website scaffold with a landing page and an About page. Built with
TanStack Start, React, Effect and native Alchemy on Cloudflare. The scaffold
includes a checked HTTP API, RPC, read-only MCP, SEO/AEO discovery files,
agent discovery (named AI crawler rules with Content Signals, an Agent Skills
index, an MCP server card and in-browser WebMCP tools) and generated social
images, all using the same dummy page content.

## Run locally

Use Bun 1.4.2 and Node 24. The lockfile pins every package resolution.

```sh
bun install --frozen-lockfile
bun run references:sync
bun run dev
```

Open <http://127.0.0.1:3210>. `dev` runs native Alchemy with the explicit
`dev` stage and Doppler config `common-practice/dev`. Sign in to Doppler locally first;
Common Practice has its own configured development credential.

The matching API runs at <http://127.0.0.1:3211>. Both apps run through native
Alchemy; there is no single-app backend fallback.
The workspace includes Bun 1.4.2 as a development dependency; use
`./node_modules/.bin/bun` if the global Bun version is older.

```sh
bun run verification
```

This builds the generated route tree, checks formatting, runs strict Oxlint and
Effect diagnostics, checks TypeScript, runs tests, checks unused files and
validates the documentation index.

## Repository map

- `apps/web`: the standard TanStack frontend and browser WebMCP host.
- `apps/api`: the native Effect API Worker, publishing routes and image renderer.
- `content/pages`: authored Markdown in `@content/pages`.
- `packages`: shared Content, HTTP, RPC, MCP, analytics and infrastructure owners.
- `alchemy.run.ts`: native Alchemy entry point for the `daw` Website and Backend stack.
- `alchemy.axiom.run.ts` and `alchemy.trace.run.ts`: the production-only
  `daw-observability` and `daw-trace-export` stacks.
- `alchemy.posthog.run.ts`: the `daw-analytics` stack for Common Practice production/Preview
  projects, dashboards and their charts.
- `test`: the opt-in Alchemy integration suite.
- `.github/workflows`: verification checks, pull-request Preview and manual production
  deployments.
- `docs`: the [documentation index](docs/README.md): design, runbooks, standards and dated evidence.
- `tools`: Effect command programs and lint enforcement tests.
- `.references`: ignored, locked upstream Effect and Alchemy source clones.
- `.agents/skills`: portable implementation guidance; `.claude/skills` links here.

Read [architecture](ARCHITECTURE.md), [documentation](docs/README.md),
[lint policy](docs/standards/lint.md), [dependency choices](docs/standards/dependencies.md)
and the [deployment runbook](docs/runbooks/deployment.md).

The wording and visual treatment are placeholders for scaffolding. Search
engines may index the production pages while that wording remains in place.
Cloudflare keeps its native Preview out of search results. The header, home artwork, favicon and social images use the approved Common
Practice tile and outlined wordmark.

## AI work history

[Entire](https://entire.io) records both Codex and Claude Code chats and tool
activity alongside Git commits. This repository was configured with Entire CLI
0.11.3. Install Entire on each machine, then run from this checkout:

```sh
entire enable --agent codex --telemetry=false --absolute-git-hook-path
entire enable --agent claude-code --telemetry=false --absolute-git-hook-path
entire status
```

Open `/hooks` in Codex and approve the seven Entire commands. Both Codex and
Claude Code must start a fresh chat after setup so Entire can record each chat
from the beginning. `entire doctor` checks the installed commands and their
approval records.

The shared configuration is in `.entire/settings.json`, `.codex/hooks.json` and
`.claude/settings.json`. Run the setup commands above in every clone, so Git's
automatic recording commands are installed there too. Entire's local logs,
working chat copies and machine-specific settings are ignored by Git. Anonymous
usage reporting is off.

Commits create checkpoints, stored as separate Git references. Pushing to
`origin` also syncs those checkpoints, including chat text and tool activity.
Commit linking is automatic (`commit_linking: "always"`). For chats that change
files, finish the normal workflow with `git commit` and `git push origin`; the
installed Git commands create and upload the record. Ending a chat alone does
not publish it online. Chats without a file change can be published using the
explicit backfill workflow below.
This follows [Entire's documented workflow](https://docs.entire.io/quickstart).
Entire removes detected secrets before saving checkpoints, but this check can
miss things. Keep credentials out of chats and review what you share. Existing
chat history is not imported by the setup command above.

The repository's Entire page is <https://entire.io/gh/crcorbett/common-practice>. Its hosted
connection keeps a private copy of the repository in Australia (Sydney). This
connection is separate from the local recording setup. This checkout's `origin`
uses the Sydney mirror; the direct GitHub URL is preserved as `upstream`. The
mirror sends ordinary code pushes through to GitHub and stores chat records.
To configure another clone for the same mirror, run:

```sh
git remote rename origin upstream
entire repo remote add origin /gh/crcorbett/common-practice --cluster aws-ap-southeast-2.entire.io
```

### Backfill existing chats

Entire CLI 0.10.5 can import existing Codex and Claude Code transcripts as
read-only checkpoints. Run a preview before importing:

```sh
entire import codex --dry-run
entire import claude-code --dry-run
entire import codex
entire import claude-code
```

The importer normally reads files changed in the past 30 days. It skips turns
already imported. Use `--session <id>` to select particular chats and `--path`
to select a transcript folder. Codex matches each chat's recorded working
folder; its default scan misses compressed archives and Common Practice's former Google
Drive location. The September 2026 backfill uses temporary, decompressed copies
of the selected chats, with only their initial working-folder field changed to
this checkout. Originals stay untouched. Claude Code's former project folder
can be selected directly with `--path`.

Imported chats can be searched and read, but cannot be resumed through Entire.
Sync them with the installed command `entire hooks git pre-push origin`, then
check the hosted Sessions page. This sync uploads checkpoint data without
pushing source changes. Use the Sydney mirror for `origin`: the initial backfill
reached GitHub, but its checkpoint references did not reach the hosted Sessions
page until they were pushed directly to the mirror. Ordinary Claude web, desktop
and Cowork chats have no direct importer in this CLI version.

## Live preview

The scaffold uses a native Cloudflare Worker Preview, managed by Alchemy, at
<https://preview-common-practice-production.coopercorbett.workers.dev>. Home and About are ready to build
on. See the deployment runbook for Doppler configuration and the reviewed
plan/deploy process.

Each same-repository pull request gets its own native Preview, stage
`pr-<number>`, deployed by the **Pull request preview** workflow. The workflow
comments the Preview URL on the pull request and destroys the Preview when the
pull request closes. Fork pull requests are skipped.

`bun run test:integration` deploys the `integration` Preview, checks Home,
About, a missing page and the matching API’s `/pages`, then destroys it. It changes
Cloudflare, needs Doppler's `common-practice/stg_preview` credentials and is not part of
`verification`; run it only with authorisation.

## Production

Private source repository: <https://github.com/crcorbett/common-practice>.
Live website: <https://withcommonpractice.com>.
API: <https://api.withcommonpractice.com>; RPC `/rpc`, remote MCP `/mcp`.
Production uses stage `production` and Doppler config `common-practice/prd`:

```sh
bun run production:plan
bun run production:deploy --yes
```

GitHub Actions has a manual **Deploy production** workflow on `main`. It checks
the selected commit and uses the same native Alchemy scripts and cloud state.
See the deployment runbook for credential rotation and deployment coordination.

## Observability

Product analytics uses PostHog separately from request telemetry. The browser's
existing Effect Atom runtime records explicit page views and selected navigation
automatically on enabled deployments, while honouring Do Not Track. Browser
batches pass through `/ingest/e/` on the Website to reduce domain blocking;
occasional loss remains possible. The API counts its own requests and completed content reads,
with short sends in native Alchemy background work. Ordinary Previews and local
development keep collection off. A separate Alchemy stack owns production/Preview
PostHog projects and two private dashboards in each. See the

## AI work history

[Entire](https://entire.io) records both Codex and Claude Code chats and tool
activity alongside Git commits. This repository was configured with Entire CLI
0.11.3. Install Entire on each machine, then run from this checkout:

```sh
entire enable --agent codex --telemetry=false --absolute-git-hook-path
entire enable --agent claude-code --telemetry=false --absolute-git-hook-path
entire status
```

Open `/hooks` in Codex and approve the seven Entire commands. Both Codex and
Claude Code must start a fresh chat after setup so Entire can record each chat
from the beginning. `entire doctor` checks the installed commands and their
approval records.

The shared configuration is in `.entire/settings.json`, `.codex/hooks.json` and
`.claude/settings.json`. Run the setup commands above in every clone, so Git's
automatic recording commands are installed there too. Entire's local logs,
working chat copies and machine-specific settings are ignored by Git. Anonymous
usage reporting is off.

Commits create checkpoints, stored as separate Git references. Pushing to
`origin` also syncs those checkpoints, including chat text and tool activity.
Commit linking is automatic (`commit_linking: "always"`). For chats that change
files, finish the normal workflow with `git commit` and `git push origin`; the
installed Git commands create and upload the record. Ending a chat alone does
not publish it online. Chats without a file change can be published using the
explicit backfill workflow below.
This follows [Entire's documented workflow](https://docs.entire.io/quickstart).
Entire removes detected secrets before saving checkpoints, but this check can
miss things. Keep credentials out of chats and review what you share. Existing
chat history is not imported by the setup command above.

The repository's Entire page is <https://entire.io/gh/crcorbett/common-practice>. Its hosted
connection keeps a private copy of the repository in Australia (Sydney). This
connection is separate from the local recording setup. This checkout's `origin`
uses the Sydney mirror; the direct GitHub URL is preserved as `upstream`. The
mirror sends ordinary code pushes through to GitHub and stores chat records.
To configure another clone for the same mirror, run:

```sh
git remote rename origin upstream
entire repo remote add origin /gh/crcorbett/common-practice --cluster aws-ap-southeast-2.entire.io
```

### Backfill existing chats

Entire CLI 0.10.5 can import existing Codex and Claude Code transcripts as
read-only checkpoints. Run a preview before importing:

```sh
entire import codex --dry-run
entire import claude-code --dry-run
entire import codex
entire import claude-code
```

The importer normally reads files changed in the past 30 days. It skips turns
already imported. Use `--session <id>` to select particular chats and `--path`
to select a transcript folder. Codex matches each chat's recorded working
folder; its default scan misses compressed archives and Common Practice's former Google
Drive location. The September 2026 backfill uses temporary, decompressed copies
of the selected chats, with only their initial working-folder field changed to
this checkout. Originals stay untouched. Claude Code's former project folder
can be selected directly with `--path`.

Imported chats can be searched and read, but cannot be resumed through Entire.
Sync them with the installed command `entire hooks git pre-push origin`, then
check the hosted Sessions page. This sync uploads checkpoint data without
pushing source changes. Use the Sydney mirror for `origin`: the initial backfill
reached GitHub, but its checkpoint references did not reach the hosted Sessions
page until they were pushed directly to the mirror. Ordinary Claude web, desktop
and Cowork chats have no direct importer in this CLI version.

## Live preview

The scaffold uses a native Cloudflare Worker Preview, managed by Alchemy, at
<https://preview-common-practice-production.coopercorbett.workers.dev>. Home and About are ready to build
on. See the deployment runbook for Doppler configuration and the reviewed
plan/deploy process.

Each same-repository pull request gets its own native Preview, stage
`pr-<number>`, deployed by the **Pull request preview** workflow. The workflow
comments the Preview URL on the pull request and destroys the Preview when the
pull request closes. Fork pull requests are skipped.

`bun run test:integration` deploys the `integration` Preview, checks Home,
About, a missing page and the matching API’s `/pages`, then destroys it. It changes
Cloudflare, needs Doppler's `common-practice/stg_preview` credentials and is not part of
`verification`; run it only with authorisation.

## Production

Private source repository: <https://github.com/crcorbett/common-practice>.
Live website: <https://withcommonpractice.com>.
API: <https://api.withcommonpractice.com>; RPC `/rpc`, remote MCP `/mcp`.
Production uses stage `production` and Doppler config `common-practice/prd`:

```sh
bun run production:plan
bun run production:deploy --yes
```

GitHub Actions has a manual **Deploy production** workflow on `main`. It checks
the selected commit and uses the same native Alchemy scripts and cloud state.
See the deployment runbook for credential rotation and deployment coordination.

# PostHog analytics in a separate Website and API

Use this when adding browser and backend analytics to the repository pattern.
This is an optional capability, not part of every generated scaffold. Start from
the questions, collection policy and accepted loss budget, then follow the
[Alchemy resource guide](../providers/posthog.md) and
[Effect browser adapter](../../../effect-client-wrapper/references/posthog-browser.md).
Keep product analytics separate from request logs, traces and operational metrics.
Apply the sibling [strict Effect policy](../../../strict-effect-ts/SKILL.md) to
schemas, services, adapters, infrastructure and tests; the SDK does not grant a
whole analytics folder an exception.

## Contents

- [Put each responsibility with its owner](#put-each-responsibility-with-its-owner)
- [Make the Effect contract reviewable](#make-the-effect-contract-reviewable)
- [Count backend work separately](#count-backend-work-separately)
- [Keep a browser relay on the owning Website](#keep-a-browser-relay-on-the-owning-website)
- [Verify the assembled capability](#verify-the-assembled-capability)

## Put each responsibility with its owner

Adapt these paths to the target repository; they are an ownership map rather
than a requirement to create every file:

```text
packages/analytics/src/
  schemas.ts                 checked settings, event vocabulary and brands
  errors.ts                  closed capture failures
  service.ts                 named browser/backend operations
  live.layer.ts              native backend HTTP capture
  test.layer.ts              deterministic service implementation
packages/infrastructure/src/posthog/
  schemas.ts / errors.ts / service.ts
  management.adapter.layer.ts  private Distilled operations and credentials
  resources.ts / dashboards.ts  resource lifecycle and desired chart catalogue
  bindings.egress.ts            checked stage-specific deployment outputs
apps/web/src/lib/analytics/
  browser.adapter.layer.ts   private SDK lifecycle
  capture.consumer.ts        synchronous checked before-send callback
  relay/
    schemas.ts / errors.ts / service.ts
    live.layer.ts            one native outbound HTTP attempt
    body.ingress.ts          bounded byte reader
    request.ingress.ts       checked Website HTTP request
    response.egress.ts       native response adaptation
apps/api/src/
  analytics.layer.ts         request-scoped collection and finalisation
alchemy.posthog.run.ts       composition-only resource stack
```

Packages import explicit package exports and never app internals. The existing
server runtime composes the relay service; the React-owned Atom runtime composes
the browser service. The native API entry composes backend capture with its
incoming request Effect fibre. No analytics package starts a runtime or shares
mutable per-request state across users.

## Make the Effect contract reviewable

- Public operations return `Effect.Effect<Success, AnalyticsError, never>` with
  Schema-derived inputs and outputs. Capture transport, configuration and SDK
  dependencies in the Layer; typecheck the real implementation against
  `Service.of`. Native request handlers may retain documented host requirements;
  those requirements must not leak into the shared analytics service.
- Use named `Effect.fn("Service.operation")` with a generator directly for
  sequential public work. Use `Effect.fnUntraced` for reusable private work that
  belongs to the caller's span. Keep pure total transformations plain. Split
  files by schema/error/service/transport ownership, not one helper per SDK call.
- Decode stage, host, token and collection mode with their owning Schema.
  Model enabled/disabled settings as a closed union: disabled needs no fake key
  or placeholder host. Invalid enabled settings are a named configuration
  failure, not configured-off. If startup must remain available, make the
  downgrade a reported policy at composition, separate from deliberate disable.
- Decode external absence to `Option` once and prefer `Option.match` for both
  branches. Do not access `.value`, inspect `_tag` or use unsafe extraction.
  Use `Boolean.match` for boolean choices and `Match.exhaustive` for closed
  states; do not introduce Option solely to hide a boolean decision. Return
  nullable values only at a host contract that explicitly requires them.
- Decode incoming data and encode owned outgoing payloads in their ingress and
  egress owners. No assertions, raw JSON, raw fetch, ambient environment reads,
  clocks, timers, random globals or raw Promise orchestration. The browser's
  named SDK adapter and synchronous consumer are the documented host exceptions;
  backend HttpClient and Distilled calls remain native Effect.
- Map expected SDK/HTTP/codec failures to closed Schema-tagged errors with safe
  operation/reason fields. Best-effort capture catches those named errors at
  its application owner. Do not erase configuration, permission or decode
  failure with blanket `Effect.option`/`Effect.ignore`, convert it with `orDie`,
  or catch all Causes to report success. Preserve interruption and defects.
  Discarding an invalid optional campaign field is a separate, explicit policy.
- Create `Ref`s and any concurrency limits during the intended Layer/request
  lifetime. Use scoped acquisition and bounded finalisers. No mutable module
  client, request accumulator, per-click runner or detached fibre. Logging and
  span fields use safe fixed names; event bodies and visitor IDs stay out.

## Count backend work separately

Collect a bounded set of domain outcomes in a request-local `Ref`, then send one
request-completed event and those outcomes together. Define whether health,
preflight, discovery and streamed responses count. Pick a truthful completion
point for streams and cancellation; do not count a stream twice or claim the
body was delivered merely because response headers exist.

Use native Effect `HttpClient` for capture rather than adding a server SDK solely
to send batches. Check and encode the owned wire Schema; distinguish accepted
HTTP responses, rejection and transport failure. Bound the entire send and keep
resources scoped. Use Effect Clock/Random for timing and event identity; do not
introduce ambient clocks or random globals. Worker CPU timing can differ from
provider-measured latency, so name the recorded duration accurately.

On native Alchemy Cloudflare Workers, use the installed
`WorkerExecutionContext.waitUntil(effect)` API for bounded background sends.
It extends request work and preserves the native Effect context without a new
runner in owned code. Call it while the native request context is valid. The
installed Alchemy implementation captures the calling services; it does not
extend every service's acquisition scope. Close over only dependencies that
remain alive for the send and open the HTTP send scope inside the background
Effect. Do not carry a soon-to-close request scope or raw host context into a
second runtime. Test request finalisation while the controlled send is pending.
It is not a persistent queue or a promise of delivery after termination.
Expected analytics failure should not change the application's response when
best-effort loss is the agreed policy. Keep fixed safe diagnostics and separate
backend request IDs from browser visitor IDs. Do not add retries without deciding
how duplicates are prevented and how long sends may live.

## Keep a browser relay on the owning Website

For a minimal browser client, an existing Website path such as `/ingest/e/` avoids
another Worker and cross-origin delivery to `api.<domain>`. A thin TanStack route
calls a native Effect HTTP program through the existing server runner. This is
fixed provider ingress for the Website's browser client, not a domain API or a

Common Practice is live at <https://withcommonpractice.com>, with its API at
<https://api.withcommonpractice.com>. The repository, packages, Workers, bindings,
Doppler project and active artwork now use the new name. Old website links redirect
with their path and query; the old API stays available for existing clients.
See the [cutover checklist](docs/exec-plans/common-practice-cutover-checklist.md)
for completed work, retained historical identifiers and the remaining external items.

A small website scaffold with a landing page and an About page. Built with
TanStack Start, React, Effect and native Alchemy on Cloudflare. The scaffold
includes a checked HTTP API, RPC, read-only MCP, SEO/AEO discovery files,
agent discovery (named AI crawler rules with Content Signals, an Agent Skills
index, an MCP server card and in-browser WebMCP tools) and generated social
images, all using the same dummy page content.

## Run locally

Use Bun 1.4.2 and Node 24. The lockfile pins every package resolution.

```sh
bun install --frozen-lockfile
bun run references:sync
bun run dev
```

Open <http://127.0.0.1:3210>. `dev` runs native Alchemy with the explicit
`dev` stage and Doppler config `common-practice/dev`. Sign in to Doppler locally first;
Common Practice has its own configured development credential.

The matching API runs at <http://127.0.0.1:3211>. Both apps run through native
Alchemy; there is no single-app backend fallback.
The workspace includes Bun 1.4.2 as a development dependency; use
`./node_modules/.bin/bun` if the global Bun version is older.

```sh
bun run verification
```

This builds the generated route tree, checks formatting, runs strict Oxlint and
Effect diagnostics, checks TypeScript, runs tests, checks unused files and
validates the documentation index.

## Repository map

- `apps/web`: the standard TanStack frontend and browser WebMCP host.
- `apps/api`: the native Effect API Worker, publishing routes and image renderer.
- `content/pages`: authored Markdown in `@content/pages`.
- `packages`: shared Content, HTTP, RPC, MCP, analytics and infrastructure owners.
- `alchemy.run.ts`: native Alchemy entry point for the `daw` Website and Backend stack.
- `alchemy.axiom.run.ts` and `alchemy.trace.run.ts`: the production-only
  `daw-observability` and `daw-trace-export` stacks.
- `alchemy.posthog.run.ts`: the `daw-analytics` stack for Common Practice production/Preview
  projects, dashboards and their charts.
- `test`: the opt-in Alchemy integration suite.
- `.github/workflows`: verification checks, pull-request Preview and manual production
  deployments.
- `docs`: the [documentation index](docs/README.md): design, runbooks, standards and dated evidence.
- `tools`: Effect command programs and lint enforcement tests.
- `.references`: ignored, locked upstream Effect and Alchemy source clones.
- `.agents/skills`: portable implementation guidance; `.claude/skills` links here.

Read [architecture](ARCHITECTURE.md), [documentation](docs/README.md),
[lint policy](docs/standards/lint.md), [dependency choices](docs/standards/dependencies.md)
and the [deployment runbook](docs/runbooks/deployment.md).

The wording and visual treatment are placeholders for scaffolding. Search
engines may index the production pages while that wording remains in place.
Cloudflare keeps its native Preview out of search results. The header, home artwork, favicon and social images use the approved Common
Practice tile and outlined wordmark.

## AI work history

[Entire](https://entire.io) records both Codex and Claude Code chats and tool
activity alongside Git commits. This repository was configured with Entire CLI
0.11.3. Install Entire on each machine, then run from this checkout:

```sh
entire enable --agent codex --telemetry=false --absolute-git-hook-path
entire enable --agent claude-code --telemetry=false --absolute-git-hook-path
entire status
```

Open `/hooks` in Codex and approve the seven Entire commands. Both Codex and
Claude Code must start a fresh chat after setup so Entire can record each chat
from the beginning. `entire doctor` checks the installed commands and their
approval records.

The shared configuration is in `.entire/settings.json`, `.codex/hooks.json` and
`.claude/settings.json`. Run the setup commands above in every clone, so Git's
automatic recording commands are installed there too. Entire's local logs,
working chat copies and machine-specific settings are ignored by Git. Anonymous
usage reporting is off.

Commits create checkpoints, stored as separate Git references. Pushing to
`origin` also syncs those checkpoints, including chat text and tool activity.
Commit linking is automatic (`commit_linking: "always"`). For chats that change
files, finish the normal workflow with `git commit` and `git push origin`; the
installed Git commands create and upload the record. Ending a chat alone does
not publish it online. Chats without a file change can be published using the
explicit backfill workflow below.
This follows [Entire's documented workflow](https://docs.entire.io/quickstart).
Entire removes detected secrets before saving checkpoints, but this check can
miss things. Keep credentials out of chats and review what you share. Existing
chat history is not imported by the setup command above.

The repository's Entire page is <https://entire.io/gh/crcorbett/common-practice>. Its hosted
connection keeps a private copy of the repository in Australia (Sydney). This
connection is separate from the local recording setup. This checkout's `origin`
uses the Sydney mirror; the direct GitHub URL is preserved as `upstream`. The
mirror sends ordinary code pushes through to GitHub and stores chat records.
To configure another clone for the same mirror, run:

```sh
git remote rename origin upstream
entire repo remote add origin /gh/crcorbett/common-practice --cluster aws-ap-southeast-2.entire.io
```

### Backfill existing chats

Entire CLI 0.10.5 can import existing Codex and Claude Code transcripts as
read-only checkpoints. Run a preview before importing:

```sh
entire import codex --dry-run
entire import claude-code --dry-run
entire import codex
entire import claude-code
```

The importer normally reads files changed in the past 30 days. It skips turns
already imported. Use `--session <id>` to select particular chats and `--path`
to select a transcript folder. Codex matches each chat's recorded working
folder; its default scan misses compressed archives and Common Practice's former Google
Drive location. The September 2026 backfill uses temporary, decompressed copies
of the selected chats, with only their initial working-folder field changed to
this checkout. Originals stay untouched. Claude Code's former project folder
can be selected directly with `--path`.

Imported chats can be searched and read, but cannot be resumed through Entire.
Sync them with the installed command `entire hooks git pre-push origin`, then
check the hosted Sessions page. This sync uploads checkpoint data without
pushing source changes. Use the Sydney mirror for `origin`: the initial backfill
reached GitHub, but its checkpoint references did not reach the hosted Sessions
page until they were pushed directly to the mirror. Ordinary Claude web, desktop
and Cowork chats have no direct importer in this CLI version.

## Live preview

The scaffold uses a native Cloudflare Worker Preview, managed by Alchemy, at
<https://preview-common-practice-production.coopercorbett.workers.dev>. Home and About are ready to build
on. See the deployment runbook for Doppler configuration and the reviewed
plan/deploy process.

Each same-repository pull request gets its own native Preview, stage
`pr-<number>`, deployed by the **Pull request preview** workflow. The workflow
comments the Preview URL on the pull request and destroys the Preview when the
pull request closes. Fork pull requests are skipped.

`bun run test:integration` deploys the `integration` Preview, checks Home,
About, a missing page and the matching API’s `/pages`, then destroys it. It changes

`verification`; run it only with authorisation.

Private source repository: <https://github.com/crcorbett/common-practice>.
Live website: <https://withcommonpractice.com>.
API: <https://api.withcommonpractice.com>; RPC `/rpc`, remote MCP `/mcp`.
Production uses stage `production` and Doppler config `common-practice/prd`:

```sh
bun run production:plan
bun run production:deploy --yes
```

GitHub Actions has a manual **Deploy production** workflow on `main`. It checks
the selected commit and uses the same native Alchemy scripts and cloud state.
See the deployment runbook for credential rotation and deployment coordination.

Product analytics uses PostHog separately from request telemetry. The browser's
existing Effect Atom runtime records explicit page views and selected navigation
automatically on enabled deployments, while honouring Do Not Track. Browser
batches pass through `/ingest/e/` on the Website to reduce domain blocking;
occasional loss remains possible. The API counts its own requests and completed content reads,
with short sends in native Alchemy background work. Ordinary Previews and local
development keep collection off. A separate Alchemy stack owns production/Preview
PostHog projects and two private dashboards in each. See the

## Owners and imports

| Owner                                                         | Responsibility                                                                                                                 |
| ------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `content/pages` — `@content/pages`                            | Authored Markdown files, YAML metadata and source inventory                                                                    |
| `packages/content` — `@common-practice/content`               | Checked Page, PublishedPage, formats, errors, Content service, live/test Layers, parsing, publication metadata and image cache |
| `packages/http` — `@common-practice/http`                     | Native HTTP contract, handlers, clients, status mapping and shared response headers                                            |
| `packages/rpc` — `@common-practice/rpc`                       | Native RPC contract, handlers and client Layer                                                                                 |
| `packages/mcp` — `@common-practice/mcp`                       | Shared tool definitions/handlers, native remote MCP, resources, prompt and discovery card                                      |
| `packages/analytics` — `@common-practice/analytics`           | Checked capture settings, event vocabulary, closed browser/backend services and bounded native HTTP capture                    |
| `packages/infrastructure` — `@common-practice/infrastructure` | Shared deployment schemas, telemetry stacks, zone ownership, request observation and isolate identity                          |
| `apps/api` — `@common-practice/api`                           | Bundle authored sources, private Takumi renderer, API composition, publishing/discovery routes and native Worker               |
| `apps/web` — `@common-practice/web`                           | TanStack HTML, navigation, page heads, error states, private binding adapter and browser WebMCP host                           |

Each package has explicit source exports and no runtime of its own. Imports
between workspaces use those exports. No package imports an app. The root Bun
catalogs own exact shared versions. All owned code, including tests and
infrastructure, follows the strict Effect skill.

```mermaid
  Agent[HTTP / RPC / MCP agent] --> Handler[Shared transport handler]
  Client --> Handler
  Handler --> Content[Content service and live Layer]
  Sources[Bundled authored Markdown] --> Content
  Content --> Image[Checked page sent to private renderer]
```

The API imports raw Markdown using Alchemy's native `?raw` loader. Content's
`live.layer.ts` parses and checks it once when the Layer is built. Invalid
metadata, unsupported Markdown or duplicate identities stop startup with a
named error. No source files are read during a request. The supported scaffold
body is one matching heading, one paragraph and its placeholder notice.

`Content.getPage({ id, format })` is one operation. Omitted `format` means
`data`, a complete PublishedPage with content, Markdown/image addresses and
search metadata. Explicit `markdown`, `og` and `seo` formats return those views.
Every response repeats `format`. Literal/default inputs have exact types;
a runtime choice returns a union that narrows when its `format` is checked.
One small schema-selected operation adapter is shared by both clients and
Content; it checks that the returned variant matches the request.

Schemas, derived types and named errors belong to Content. HTTP, RPC and MCP
reuse them. The native builders validate requests and encode outputs. Image
bytes use Effect's base64 codec on JSON transports and decode to checked PNG
bytes in typed clients. Expected errors decode to native tagged Effect errors.
A transport failure and an invalid response have separate named errors.

Both Content clients allow 40 seconds for each complete read, including the
reply body. Content owns this shared deadline. It leaves ten seconds beyond
the API's 30-second image limit for sending and checking the reply. Expiry
interrupts the pending call and returns the existing `ContentUnavailableError`
with its operation name; earlier caller cancellation stays interruption.
There is no automatic client retry.

Content reads a page once and passes the checked Page to its image service.
That service never calls Content. It owns a five-minute success cache, one
render permit and a 30-second timeout; failures expire immediately. The default
page response advertises the image address without rendering it. The API's
private Takumi adapter owns image SDK Promise calls. Browser PostHog calls stay
in the Website's private analytics adapter; backend capture uses native Effect
HttpClient rather than another SDK or Promise runner.

## Runtime and frontend loading

`apps/api/src/deployment/cloudflare/worker.ts` uses Alchemy's native Worker
class-and-`make` pattern. The lightweight class keeps the renderer and server
implementation out of Website bindings. Its native runtime builds Content,
images and routes once per isolate. `apps/api/src/application.layer.ts` checks
the API address and builds the native handler in Alchemy's instance Scope.
Shared services stay alive until that instance stops. Each request runs in its incoming Effect
fibre with its own cancellation, tracer and Scope. Streamed responses retain
that Scope until completion or cancellation. There is no API ManagedRuntime
or extra Promise runner.

Native Alchemy planning registers that Worker and its telemetry. It skips runtime
binding reads because Alchemy resolves `Worker.URL` only before upload. The native

the uploaded bundle, so startup never asks for stack-only Stage or Zone services.
The native
`ALCHEMY_PHASE` selects startup of the real application after Alchemy supplies the
running Worker's checked bindings. Source validation and native bundle tests are
local proof; the public suite checks the uploaded application.

The Website keeps one server runtime at `apps/web/src/lib/runtime.server.ts`.
Every TanStack entry point uses its one runner and incoming cancellation signal.
`api/binding.adapter.layer.ts` immediately converts Cloudflare's required
service-binding Promise into Effect. It preserves the body stream and passes
Effect's abort signal; it does not clone the Request. The native HTTP client
provides the same Content service contract to page loaders. There is no local
backend fallback and no Effect Context passed through TanStack.

through TanStack's JSON serialisation, instead of throwing an error whose useful
fields would be lost. Routes render returned page text and metadata, or a named
error state. The Website has no authored page records or image renderer.

initialise its Atom. The browser uses the public native HTTP client, with no
credentials and no redirects, and the same shared tool handlers. Unmounting
closes the tool registration Scope. `browser-atom.ts` reaches this runtime only
inside TanStack's client environment function; server rendering mounts an inert
Atom. No browser global is read during import.

The WebMCP host adapter registers only when the browser's exact origin matches
the deployed Website's checked self address. This includes its matching Preview
and local address. Remote MCP has a separate public Origin policy.

The only command runtimes are `tools/references/sync.runtime.ts` and
`tools/checks/docs.runtime.ts`. Tests run through `@effect/vitest`. Host Promise
exceptions are limited to the Website runner, its Cloudflare binding/span
adapter, the private Takumi adapter, the browser WebMCP host and the private
browser analytics adapter. PostHog's synchronous before-send callback is an
exact consumer: it returns a checked event containing only allowed fields, or
null. It never runs another Effect runtime.

| Website                                                        | API                                |
| -------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------- |
| `/`, `/about` HTML                                             | `/pages`, `/pages/:id?format=data` |
| `/index.md`, `/about.md`                                       | `/pages/:id?format=markdown`       |
| `/.og`, `/about.og`                                            | `/pages/:id?format=og`             |
| HTML page heads                                                | `/pages/:id?format=seo`            |
| robots, sitemap, llms text, API catalogue, skills and MCP card | `/openapi.json`, `/rpc`, `/mcp`    |

Production's API base address is `https://api.withcommonpractice.com`.
The old API address remains a serving alias for existing clients.
The Website keeps canonical HTML, Markdown and image URLs. Discovery files and
cards advertise their own stage's API. Website representation routes choose
Content's requested format. Discovery routes forward through the same private
binding to API-owned publishing code. Legacy Website `/api/*`, `/rpc` and `/mcp`
routes are removed without aliases or redirects.

HTTP and RPC are public read-only APIs with credential-free CORS. The API allows
native Effect's `b3` and `traceparent` request headers, so the browser Content
client can read pages without disabling tracing. Remote MCP is anonymous and
broadly accessible to compatible agents, including valid
third-party browser origins. Its native transport supports the published
`2026-07-28` protocol. It accepts absent Origin or a valid serialised HTTP(S)
origin and rejects malformed or opaque origins before CORS, including preflight
requests. A small pinned Effect patch lets the existing native Origin check use
a checked predicate; no transport validation is bypassed. Compatibility and
connect/list/call behaviour require their own public checks.

can recognise an unchanged address while planning. An Action output would stay
unresolved and make that binding appear changed on every plan.

L301: # Send OpenTelemetry data to Axiom
L302: 
L303: Learn how OpenTelemetry-compatible events flow into Axiom and explore Axiom comprehensive observability through browsing, querying, dashboards, and alerting of OpenTelemetry data.
L304: 
L305: OpenTelemetry (OTel) is a set of APIs, libraries, and agents to capture distributed traces and metrics from your app. It’s a Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) project that was started to create a unified solution for service and app performance monitoring.
L306: The OpenTelemetry project has published strong specifications for the three main pillars of observability: logs, traces, and metrics. These schemas are supported by all tools and services that support interacting with OpenTelemetry. Axiom supports OpenTelemetry natively on an API level, allowing you to connect any existing OpenTelemetry shipper, library, or tool to Axiom for sending data.
L307: OpenTelemetry-compatible events flow into Axiom, where they’re organized into datasets for easy segmentation. Users can create a dataset to receive OpenTelemetry data and obtain an API token for ingestion. Axiom provides comprehensive observability through browsing, querying, dashboards, and alerting of OpenTelemetry data.
L308: 
L309: OpenTelemetry component  | Support
L310: --- | ---
L311: cite134†Logs†opentelemetry.io | ✓
L312: cite135†Traces†opentelemetry.io | ✓
L313: cite136†Metrics†opentelemetry.io | ✓
L314: 
L315: Info
L316: You must use a different, dedicated dataset for each OTel component. When you create a dataset, select Events for logs or traces data, and select Metrics for metrics data. For more information, see cite137†Create dataset .
L317: ## cite138†Prerequisites L318: 
L319:   * cite139†Create an Axiom account†app.axiom.co .
L320:   * cite137†Create a dataset in Axiom where you send your data.
L321:   * cite67†Create an API token in Axiom with permissions to ingest data to the dataset you have created.
L322: ## cite140†OpenTelemetry Collector L323: 
L324: Configuring the OpenTelemetry collector is as simple as creating an HTTP exporter that sends data to the Axiom API together with headers to set the dataset and API token.
L325: 
L326: [Button: Logs][Button: Traces][Button: Metrics]
L327: YAML
L328: 
L329:     `exporters:
L330:       otlphttp:
L331:         compression: zstd
L332:         endpoint: https://AXIOM_DOMAIN
L333:         headers:
L334:           authorization: Bearer API_TOKEN
L335:           x-axiom-dataset: DATASET_NAME
L336: 
L337:     service:
L338:       pipelines:
L339:         logs:
L340:           receivers:
L341:             - otlp
L342:           processors:
L343:             - memory_limiter
L344:             - batch
L345:           exporters:
L346:             - otlphttp`
L347: YAML
L348: 
L349:     `exporters:
L350:       otlphttp:
L351:         compression: zstd
L352:         endpoint: https://AXIOM_DOMAIN
L353:         headers:
L354:           authorization: Bearer API_TOKEN
L355:           x-axiom-dataset: DATASET_NAME
L356: 
L357:     service:
L358:       pipelines:
L359:         traces:
L360:           receivers:
L361:             - otlp
L362:           processors:
L363:             - memory_limiter
L364:             - batch
L365:           exporters:
L366:             - otlphttp`
L367: YAML
L368: 
L369:     `processors:
L370:       batch:
L371:         send_batch_max_size: 8192
L372: 
L373:     exporters:
L374:       otlphttp:
L375:         compression: zstd
L376:         endpoint: https://AXIOM_DOMAIN
L377:         headers:
L378:           authorization: Bearer API_TOKEN
L379:           x-axiom-metrics-dataset: DATASET_NAME
L380: 
L381:     service:
L382:       pipelines:
L383:         metrics:
L384:           receivers:
L385:             - otlp
L386:           processors:
L387:             - memory_limiter
L388:             - batch
L389:           exporters:
L390:             - otlphttp`
L391: 
L392: Info
L393: Replace `AXIOM_DOMAIN` with the base domain of your edge deployment. For more information, see cite9†Edge deployments .
L394: 
L395: Replace `API_TOKEN` with the Axiom API token you have generated. For added security, store the API token in an environment variable.
L396: 
L397: Replace `DATASET_NAME` with the name of the Axiom dataset where you send your data.
L398: 
L399: When configuring metrics, use the `x-axiom-metrics-dataset` header instead of `x-axiom-dataset`.
L400: When using the OTLP/HTTP endpoint, the following endpoint URLs should be used in your SDK exporter OTel configuration.
L401: 
L402:   * Traces: `https://AXIOM_DOMAIN/v1/traces`
L403:   * Logs: `https://AXIOM_DOMAIN/v1/logs`
L404:   * Metrics: `https://AXIOM_DOMAIN/v1/metrics`
L405: 
L406: Info
L407: 
L408: The `/v1/metrics` endpoint only supports the `application/x-protobuf` content type. JSON format isn’t supported for metrics ingestion.
L409: ## cite141†OpenTelemetry for Go L410: 
L411: The example below configures a Go app using the cite142†OpenTelemetry SDK for Go†github.com to send OpenTelemetry data to Axiom.
L412: go
L413: 
L414:     `package main
L415: 
L416:     import (
L417:        "context" // For managing request-scoped values, cancellation signals, and deadlines.
L418:        "crypto/tls" // For configuring TLS options, like certificates.
L419: 
L420:        // OpenTelemetry imports for setting up tracing and exporting telemetry data.
L421:        "go.opentelemetry.io/otel" // Core OpenTelemetry APIs for managing tracers.
L422:        "go.opentelemetry.io/otel/attribute" // For creating and managing trace attributes.
L423:        "go.opentelemetry.io/otel/exporters/otlp/otlptrace/otlptracehttp" // HTTP trace exporter for OpenTelemetry Protocol (OTLP).
L424:        "go.opentelemetry.io/otel/propagation" // For managing context propagation formats.
L425:        "go.opentelemetry.io/otel/sdk/resource" // For defining resources that describe an entity producing telemetry.
L426:        "go.opentelemetry.io/otel/sdk/trace" // For configuring tracing, like sampling and processors.
L427:        semconv "go.opentelemetry.io/otel/semconv/v1.24.0" // Semantic conventions for resource attributes.
L428:     )
L429: 
L430:     const (
L431:        serviceName           = "axiom-go-otel" // Name of the service for tracing.
L432:        serviceVersion        = "0.1.0" // Version of the service.
L433:        otlpEndpoint          = "AXIOM_DOMAIN" // OTLP collector endpoint.
L434:        bearerToken           = "Bearer API_TOKEN" // Authorization token.
L435:        deploymentEnvironment = "production" // Deployment environment.
L436:     )
L437:     func SetupTracer() (func(context.Context) error, error) {
L438:        ctx := context.Background()
L439:        return InstallExportPipeline(ctx) // Setup and return the export pipeline for telemetry data.
L440:     }
L441: 
L442:     func Resource() *resource.Resource {
L443:        // Defines resource with service name, version, and environment.
L444:        return resource.NewWithAttributes(
L445:            semconv.SchemaURL,
L446:            semconv.ServiceNameKey.String(serviceName),
L447:            semconv.ServiceVersionKey.String(serviceVersion),
L448:            attribute.String("environment", deploymentEnvironment),
L449:        )
L450:     }
L451: 
L452:     func InstallExportPipeline(ctx context.Context) (func(context.Context) error, error) {
L453:        // Sets up OTLP HTTP exporter with endpoint, headers, and TLS config.
L454:        exporter, err := otlptracehttp.New(ctx,
L455:            otlptracehttp.WithEndpoint(otlpEndpoint),
L456:            otlptracehttp.WithHeaders(map[string]string{
L457:                "Authorization":   bearerToken,
L458:                "X-AXIOM-DATASET": "DATASET_NAME",
L459:            }),
L460:            otlptracehttp.WithTLSClientConfig(&tls.Config{}),
L461:        )
L462:        if err != nil {
L463:            return nil, err
L464:        }
L465: 
L466:        // Configures the tracer provider with the exporter and resource.
L467:        tracerProvider := trace.NewTracerProvider(
L468:            trace.WithBatcher(exporter),
L469:            trace.WithResource(Resource()),
L470:        )
L471:        otel.SetTracerProvider(tracerProvider)
L472: 
L473:        // Sets global propagator to W3C Trace Context and Baggage.
L474:        otel.SetTextMapPropagator(propagation.NewCompositeTextMapPropagator(
L475:            propagation.TraceContext{},
L476:            propagation.Baggage{},
L477:        ))
L478: 
L479:        return tracerProvider.Shutdown, nil // Returns a function to shut down the tracer provider.
L480:     }`
L481: Info
L482: 
L483: Replace `AXIOM_DOMAIN` with the base domain of your edge deployment. For more information, see cite9†Edge deployments .
L484: 
L485: Replace `API_TOKEN` with the Axiom API token you have generated. For added security, store the API token in an environment variable.
L486: 
L487: Replace `DATASET_NAME` with the name of the Axiom dataset where you send your data.

L521: ## cite145†OpenTelemetry for Java L522: 
L523: Here is a basic configuration for a Java app that sends traces to an OpenTelemetry Collector using OTLP over HTTP using the cite146†OpenTelemetry Java SDK†github.com :
L524: java
L525: 
L526:     `package com.example;
L527: 
L528:     import io.opentelemetry.api.OpenTelemetry;
L529:     import io.opentelemetry.api.common.Attributes;
L530:     import io.opentelemetry.api.common.AttributeKey;
L531:     import io.opentelemetry.exporter.otlp.http.trace.OtlpHttpSpanExporter;
L532:     import io.opentelemetry.sdk.OpenTelemetrySdk;
L533:     import io.opentelemetry.sdk.resources.Resource;
L534:     import io.opentelemetry.sdk.trace.SdkTracerProvider;
L535:     import io.opentelemetry.sdk.trace.export.BatchSpanProcessor;
L536:     import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit;
L537: 
L538:     public class OtelConfiguration {
L539:         // OpenTelemetry configuration
L540:         private static final String SERVICE_NAME = "SERVICE_NAME";
L541:         private static final String SERVICE_VERSION = "SERVICE_VERSION";
L542:         private static final String OTLP_ENDPOINT = "https://AXIOM_DOMAIN/v1/traces";
L543:         private static final String BEARER_TOKEN = "Bearer API_TOKEN";
L544:         private static final String AXIOM_DATASET = "DATASET_NAME";
L545:         public static OpenTelemetry initializeOpenTelemetry() {
L546:             // Create a Resource with service name and version
L547:             Resource resource = Resource.getDefault()
L548:                     .merge(Resource.create(Attributes.of(
L549:                             AttributeKey.stringKey("service.name"), SERVICE_NAME,
L550:                             AttributeKey.stringKey("service.version"), SERVICE_VERSION
L551:                     )));
L552: 
L553:             // Create an OTLP/HTTP span exporter
L554:             OtlpHttpSpanExporter spanExporter = OtlpHttpSpanExporter.builder()
L555:                     .setEndpoint(OTLP_ENDPOINT)
L556:                     .addHeader("Authorization", BEARER_TOKEN)
L557:                     .addHeader("X-Axiom-Dataset", AXIOM_DATASET)
L558:                     .build();
L559: 
L560:             // Create a BatchSpanProcessor with the OTLP/HTTP exporter
L561:             SdkTracerProvider sdkTracerProvider = SdkTracerProvider.builder()
L562:                     .addSpanProcessor(BatchSpanProcessor.builder(spanExporter)
L563:                             .setScheduleDelay(100, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)
L564:                             .build())
L565:                     .setResource(resource)
L566:                     .build();
L567: 
L568:             // Build and register the OpenTelemetry SDK
L569:             OpenTelemetrySdk openTelemetry = OpenTelemetrySdk.builder()
L570:                     .setTracerProvider(sdkTracerProvider)
L571:                     .buildAndRegisterGlobal();
L572:             // Add a shutdown hook to properly close the SDK
L573:             Runtime.getRuntime().addShutdownHook(new Thread(sdkTracerProvider::close));
L574: 
L575:             return openTelemetry;
L576:         }
L577:     }`

L581: 
L582: Replace `API_TOKEN` with the Axiom API token you have generated. For added security, store the API token in an environment variable.
L583: 
L584: Replace `DATASET_NAME` with the name of the Axiom dataset where you send your data.

#### Contents

iframe

PostHog captures two types of events: anonymous and identified

Identified events enable you to attribute events to specific users, and attach person properties. They're best suited for logged-in users.

Scenarios where you want to capture identified events are:

  * Tracking logged-in users in B2B and B2C SaaS apps
  * Doing user segmented product analysis
  * Growth and marketing teams wanting to analyze the complete conversion lifecycle

Anonymous events are events without individually identifiable data. They're best suited for web analytics or apps where users aren't logged in.

Scenarios where you want to capture anonymous events are:

  * Tracking a marketing website
  * Content-focused sites
  * B2C apps where users don't sign up or log in

Under the hood, the key difference between identified and anonymous events is that for identified events we create a person profile for the user, whereas for anonymous events we do not.

> Important: Due to the reduced cost of processing them, anonymous events can be up to 4x cheaper than identified ones, so we recommended you only capture identified events when needed.

Image: Anonymous vs identified events

## How to capture anonymous events

  * [Button: Web]

The JavaScript Web SDK captures anonymous events by default. However, this may change depending on your `person_profiles` config when initializing PostHog:

  1. `person_profiles: 'identified_only'` (recommended) (default) - Anonymous events are captured by default. PostHog only captures identified events for users where person profiles have already been created.

  2. `person_profiles: 'always'` - Capture identified events for all events.

For example:

Web
    
    `
    
    posthog.init('<ph_project_token>', {
    
        api_host: 'https://us.i.posthog.com',
    
        defaults: '2026-05-30',
    
        person_profiles: 'always'
    
    })
    
    `

PostHog's backend SDKs and API capture identified events by default. To capture anonymous events, set the `$process_person_profile` property to `false` and use a distinct ID that isn't linked to a person profile. Generate a random value, such as a UUID, and reuse it for the rest of the visit or session instead of sharing one ID like `system` across all anonymous events. Anonymous events are stored without person properties and don't link to groups, so group analytics doesn't count them. If the distinct ID already belongs to a person, the event is still linked to that person and counts as an identified event – it just can't update their person properties:

## Frequently asked questions

### General questions

What can I do with anonymous events?

You can:

  * Set event properties
  * Aggregate and filter events by event properties (e.g. URL, location, UTM source)
  * Create insights like trends, funnels, SQL insights and more

You cannot:

  * Set person properties
  * Create cohorts
  * Use Lifecycle insights
  * Filter on person properties
  * Use person properties for targeting feature flags, A/B tests, or surveys
  * Query the `persons` table using the SQL editor
  * Use group analytics
What can I do with identified events?

You can use all of PostHog's features with identified events. There are no restrictions.

What happens to events when an anonymous user is identified?

All future events are associated with their person profile and are captured and billed as identified events.

Past events are attributed to the person, but are otherwise unchanged. This means that past events remain billed as anonymous.

Can I specify some events to be identified and others to be anonymous for the same users?

Not if you already identified them. Once a user is identified, all future events for that user are associated with their person profile and are captured as identified events.

How do I revert back to anonymous events after identifying?

Calling `reset()` will unlink the person profile from the user and create a new PostHog anonymous ID for capturing events. Any future events are captured as anonymous events.

However, if you capture events using the `distinct_id` used in their previously identified person profile, the events are captured as identified events. You need to use a new `distinct_id` to capture events as anonymous events.

### Data questions

Can identified events still be "anonymous"?

Yes, identified events can still be "anonymous" in the sense that they don't need to contain personal information such as name, email, or phone number. A person profile is still created for them, but it doesn't need to include any personal information.

How are initial person properties set when an anonymous user is identified?

As person properties are not stored on anonymous events, we cannot get any initial person properties directly from those events. Instead, we retrieve the initial person properties based on the values in the persistence store.

We derive the following values from the persistence store:

  * `$initial_current_url`
  * `$initial_pathname`
  * `$initial_referrer`
  * `$initial_referring_domain`
  * `$initial_host`
  * and any initial properties that can be derived from the URL e.g., `$initial_utm_campaign`, `$initial_utm_content`, `$initial_utm_medium`, `$initial_utm_source`

Note that the above initial parameters will only work across subdomains if you're using `persistence: "localStorage+cookie"` (default) or `persistence: "cookie"`.

For cross-domain traffic, or when tracking users between web and mobile, cookie-based data wouldn't be available on the new site, so it's advised to call one of:

  * `posthog.identify()` if you have a persistent user ID available, or
  * `posthog.createPersonProfile()` if you don't have a persistent user ID. Make sure that you are bootstrapping the PostHog SDK on the new second or mobile app with the anonymous distinct ID from the first site.

Any other initial person properties, including initial GeoIP properties will be set from the values in the event at the time that the person profile was created i.e. when the events became identified.

If we change our `person_profiles` config from `identified_only'`to `always`, will we get all the person data from the previously captured anonymous events?

No, anonymous events only capture the event data and none of the person data. If that person is identified at a later date – either by identifying them or changing your configuration settings – there isn't a way to retrieve the person properties from the previously captured anonymous events.

### Insights questions

Are there any insights that behave differently?

Most insights make use of both anonymous and identified events. The exception to this is lifecycle insights, as anonymous events are excluded from this calculation. Users who first appear as 'new' might have had prior anonymous events, but their lifecycle starts only when they are identified.

Why am I seeing "Person without distinct_id" in my insights?

These are users who do not have a person profile and are anonymous users. We're aware that the wording here is confusing and are looking into updating this.

Why am I seeing drops in my insights that rely on person properties?

If you have previously had your `person_profiles` config set to `always` and your `person_profiles` config is now set to `identified_only`, you will likely see a dip in your insights graph if the filter settings include a person property.

Insights using person properties in the filter settings will essentially be filtering on identified events, where the person profile linked to that event has the relevant property set.

Changing your `person_profiles` config to `identified_only` now means that there are fewer person profiles being created and being associated with events, and therefore fewer events to be included in your insight. The person profile won't exist until the person has been identified, which may happen at a later date or not happen at all.

Depending on what you're trying to visualize, you may be able to use some of the properties on the events themselves to achieve a similar outcome – e.g. by filtering on the referring domain on the first ever pageview for each user, instead of the initial referrer person property.

### Billing questions

Why are identified events more expensive?

Since identified events are associated with a person profile, processing and querying them requires using resource intensive table JOINs. On the other hand, anonymous events are stored in a single table, and are more efficient to query. Read this post for more detail on this.

Why am I being charged for both "events" and "persons"

We're not charging you for both. The person profiles line item you see on your invoice is a number of identified events captured. The events line item is the total number of anonymous events captured.

How does my free allowance work for anonymous vs identified events?

Your first one million events each month are free, regardless if they are anonymous or identified.

# People

People in PostHog represent the users behind your events. You can view them in the People tab.

People have person profiles with properties. This enables you to do things like:

  * Filter on person properties
  * Create cohorts
  * Use person properties for targeting feature flags, A/B tests, and surveys.
  * Track initial UTM values and referrers across anonymous and identified users.
  * Query the `persons` table using SQL insights

## How to create person profiles

Person profiles are created when you capture an identified event – an event that includes identifying information like a user ID or email through the `identify` call.

### Understanding distinct IDs vs person profiles

Every event in PostHog has a distinct ID – a unique identifier that groups events together. However, not every distinct ID has a person profile:

  * Anonymous events – Events captured before `identify` is called use an anonymous distinct ID (a UUID generated by the SDK). These events are recorded but don't create a person profile.
  * Identified events – After you call `identify`, PostHog creates a person profile and links it to both the identified distinct ID and any previous anonymous events from that session.

### What happens without a person profile

If you see a UUID in the PostHog UI instead of a user's name or email, it means:

  1. The user hasn't been identified yet – they only have anonymous events
  2. No person profile exists for this distinct ID

Anonymous events are still captured and stored. When you later call `identify` for this user, PostHog automatically:

  * Creates a person profile
  * Merges the anonymous events with the identified user
  * Links the anonymous distinct ID to the person profile

### When profiles are automatically created

Person profiles are created when you:

  * Call `posthog.identify()` with a distinct ID
  * Set person properties using `posthog.setPersonProperties()`
  * Capture an event with `$set` or `$set_once` properties

`$set` and `$set_once` aren't stored on events

These properties only tell PostHog how to update person data during ingestion — they aren't kept on the stored event, so you can't filter, break down, or query events by them. To query the values you set, use person properties instead.

To control costs, you can configure anonymous vs identified events for events that don't need person profiles.

A data warehouse table can also enrich profiles that already exist. See warehouse properties. It never creates a profile, so a customer who has not used your product yet stays out of PostHog until they do.

## Duplicate person profiles

If your `identify` implementation has gaps, a single real-world user can end up with multiple person profiles. For example, if a user visits your app on a phone and a laptop but `identify` is only called on one device, each device creates its own profile with a separate anonymous distinct ID. This usually points to a misconfiguration — when `identify` is called correctly on every device and session, PostHog merges these into one profile automatically.

The most common cause of duplicate profiles is using different distinct IDs for the same user across systems without calling `alias` to link them. When PostHog can't merge two already-identified profiles, it blocks the merge and logs a "Refused to merge an already identified user" ingestion warning. If you're seeing this warning, it means your users are accumulating duplicate profiles that won't be merged automatically.

Duplicate profiles inflate counts that rely on person profiles, such as cohort sizes and feature flag targeting. If you notice these numbers are higher than expected, check your ingestion warnings and verify that you're calling `identify` as soon as a user logs in on every device and browser.

To fix existing duplicates, see how to merge users.

## The persons list

The People tab displays a list of all people in your project. By default, the list includes the following columns:

  * Person - display name for the person
  * ID - the person's distinct ID
  * Created at - when the person profile was first created
  * Last seen - when the person was last active, rounded to the nearest hour (opt-in, see below)
  * Delete - option to delete the person

You can sort the list by any column and customize which columns are visible by clicking the Configure columns button above the table.

### Last seen

The Last seen column tracks when a person was last active. This feature is opt-in — to enable it for your project, go to Settings > Product analytics > Person last seen tracking. When disabled, the column is not updated after the person is fi…448 tokens truncated…Avoid reusing deleted distinct IDs

User deletion requests are not immediate, but processed asynchronously. We recommend that you avoid reusing a deleted `distinct_id` value for a new user, as it may lead to unexpected results while the deletion is being processed. Once the deletion process is fully processed, PostHog does not retain any data associated with the deleted `distinct_id`.

If you must reuse the `distinct_id`, you can do so using the Reset deleted person tool, available from the dropdown at the top-right of the persons page. This tool enables you to reset a deleted `distinct_id` so that future events associated with it create a new person profile.

If you instead want to split a person with multiple IDs (e.g. to isolate bad data tied to a specific `distinct_id`), use the Split IDs button on their person profile.

### Via the API

You can also delete persons data via the API. When deleting a person, you can pass `delete_events=true` to delete their events and `delete_recordings=true` to delete their session recordings. Recording deletion uses crypto-shredding to permanently destroy encryption keys, making the recordings unrecoverable.

## Person profiles and properties

For backward compatibility, the Go SDK captures identified events by default. These create person profiles. To set person properties in these profiles, include them when capturing an event:

Go
    
    `
    
    client.Enqueue(posthog.Capture{
    
        DistinctId: "distinct_id",
    
        Event:      "event_name",
    
        Properties: map[string]interface{}{
    
            "$set": map[string]interface{}{
    
                "name": "Max Hedgehog",
    
            },
    
            "$set_once": map[string]interface{}{
    
                "initial_url": "/blog",
    
            },
    
        },
    
    })
    
    `

For more details on the difference between `$set` and `$set_once`, see our person properties docs.

To capture anonymous events without person profiles, set the event's `$process_person_profile` property to `false`:

Go
    
    `
    
    client.Enqueue(posthog.Capture{
    
        DistinctId: "distinct_id",
    
        Event:      "event_name",
    
        Properties: map[string]interface{}{
    
            "$process_person_profile": false,
    
        },
    
    })
    
    `

## Alias

Sometimes, you want to assign multiple distinct IDs to a single user. This is helpful when your primary distinct ID is inaccessible. For example, if a distinct ID used on the frontend is not available in your backend.

In this case, you can use `alias` to assign another distinct ID to the same user.

Go
    
    `
    
    client.Enqueue(posthog.Alias{
    
      DistinctId: "distinct_id",
    
      Alias: "alias_id",
    
    })
    
    `

We strongly recommend reading our docs on alias to best understand how to correctly use this method.

## Request context

Use request context to apply a distinct ID, session ID, and common request properties to capture and exception events inside a `net/http` request. This is useful when connecting frontend activity to backend events, session replay, error tracking, and feature flag evaluation.
By default, it also reads `X-PostHog-Distinct-Id` and `X-PostHog-Session-Id` as request-scoped defaults. Explicit `DistinctId` values and `$session_id` properties passed to captures take precedence over request context.

If request context is attached but no distinct ID is available, capture and exception events are sent as personless events with an auto-generated UUID and `$process_person_profile: false`. Calls to `Enqueue` without request context still require `DistinctId`. `EvaluateFlagsWithContext` uses the request-scoped distinct ID when `EvaluateFlagsPayload.DistinctId` is empty, but it never generates personless IDs and returns `ErrNoDistinctID` when no distinct ID is available.

Tracing headers are client-controlled analytics context, not authentication or authorization. For security-sensitive server-side decisions, pass an authenticated `DistinctId` explicitly or attach one to the request context:

Go
    
    `
    
    ctx := posthog.WithRequestContext(r.Context(), posthog.RequestContext{
    
        DistinctId: user.ID,
    
    })
    
    `

To ignore tracing headers while keeping request metadata, disable tracing header capture:

Go
    
    `
    
    handler := posthog.NewRequestContextMiddleware(
    
        next,
    
        posthog.WithCaptureTracingHeaders(false),
    
    )
    
    `

## Breakdowns

You can break down your retention numbers and graph by the following property types:

Name  | Description
--- | ---
Event properties  | Properties specific to a tracked event (e.g. `Country Name`)
Person properties  | Properties stored on a user's person profile (e.g. `company_name`)
Feature flags  | Events where a specific feature flag was enabled
Group properties  | Properties stored on a group (requires group analytics)
Cohorts  | Events performed by a pre-defined list of users
SQL expression  | A custom SQL expression for derived or computed values (e.g. `upper(properties.$browser)`)

For example, breaking down by Country Name can help you see which countries have higher retention for a feature.

When using breakdowns, you see the mean retention for each breakdown value and can click on each row to expand and show each cohort with that breakdown value. There is also a dropdown selector which lets you filter the graph and table for a specific breakdown value.

Bootstrapping with `instrumentation-client`

When using `instrumentation-client`, the values you pass to `posthog.init` remain fixed for the entire session. This means bootstrapping only works if you evaluate flags before your app renders (for example, on the server).

If you need flag values after the app has rendered, you’ll want to:

  * Evaluate the flag on the server and pass the value into your app, or
  * Evaluate the flag in an earlier page/state, then store and re-use it when needed.

Both approaches avoid flicker and give you the same outcome as bootstrapping, as long as you use the same `distinct_id` across client and server.

See the bootstrapping guide for more information.

## Identifying users

> Identifying users is required. Call `posthog.identify('your-user-id')` after login to link events to a known user. This is what connects frontend event captures, session replays, LLM traces, and error tracking to the same person — and lets backend events link back too.
> 
> Use a stable ID from your auth system when possible, not an email or display name. Send those as person properties instead. If your app has no other stable key, email works as a fallback if they are unique. Never a shared literal like `"anonymous"` or `"user"`, which pools many people onto one person and corrupts their data. --------------------------------------------------------------------------------

June 20, 2026 · Error Tracking Team · Error tracking

The Android SDK now supports exception steps for Error Tracking.

Call `PostHog.addExceptionStep("message", properties)` to record a rolling buffer of breadcrumb-style context that attaches to every `$exception` event as `$exception_steps`. The result: a timeline of activity leading up to each crash, so you know exactly what happened before things went sideways.
